opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest limitation right now isn't raw intelligence. It's everything around the model. The models are getting quite good at reasoning through a single step, but when you ask an agent to do real work over a long horizon, it's the context and the feedback loop that break down.

A few things stand out to me. First is verification. If an agent writes a hundred lines of code or makes a bunch of changes across a system, how does it, or the person, know it actually did the right thing? Humans are great at checking a small diff, but as agents take on bigger chunks of work, our ability to review becomes the bottleneck. So I think a lot of progress will come from agents that can check their own work: running tests, looking at the output, noticing when something's off, and correcting course without needing a human to babysit every step.

Second is context. The model only knows what you put in front of it. A lot of what makes a senior engineer or a good employee valuable is all the implicit knowledge: why the codebase is structured a certain way, what the team tried last quarter that didn't work, what the customer actually cares about. Getting that information to the agent at the right time, without drowning it in irrelevant stuff, is still really hard.

And third is the tools and interfaces themselves. We spend a ton of effort on prompts, but in my experience the design of the tools you give an agent matters just as much. If a tool is confusing, has ambiguous parameters, or returns a giant blob of output, the model struggles the same way a person would. Treating the agent-computer interface with the same care we give human-computer interfaces makes a huge difference.

So if I had to sum it up: the limitation is less "can the model think" and more "can we build the scaffolding, the context, and the feedback loops so it can reliably do long, messy, real-world work." That's where I think a lot of the most interesting engineering is happening right now.

r001.rationale: The response names verification, context, tools, and feedback loops as limitations, but does not identify people’s trust in agent outputs as the biggest limitation.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that agent work has little or no value to someone who cannot trust it.

r003.rationale: It discusses human review and agents checking their own work, but does not recommend making work auditable by humans as a way to establish trust.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the biggest limitation right now isn't raw intelligence, it's context. Agents are getting very good at the actual work, writing the code, running the tools, fixing the bug. But they're starting every task cold. They don't know the thing you told your coworker last week, or why that one module is structured so weirdly, or that the team already tried the obvious approach and it broke prod.

A new engineer who joins your team spends their first few months just absorbing that stuff. Right now agents never get past day one. So you end up being the bottleneck, re-explaining the same background over and over, and that caps how much work you can actually hand off.

The second piece, which is related, is verification. When an agent does ten minutes of work for you, you can read it all. When it does ten hours, you can't. So the question becomes how does it know when it's done, how does it know when it's wrong, and how does it surface the two decisions you'd actually care about out of the hundred it made. We've seen that if you give the model a way to really check its own work, a test suite, a browser it can click around in, a screenshot it can look at, the reliability jumps a lot. Without that, it's guessing, and it's often confidently guessing.

So if I had to pick one thing to work on, it's building the environment around the model, memory, tools, feedback loops, rather than just making the model smarter. The intelligence is honestly getting ahead of the scaffolding we've built for it.

r001.rationale: The response names context as the biggest limitation. It discusses verification as a related issue but does not identify trust in agent outputs as the likely biggest limitation.

r002.rationale: The response says unreliable agents may be guessing, but does not argue that their work has little or no value to someone who cannot trust it.

r003.rationale: The response recommends giving agents tools to check their own work and surface key decisions, but does not recommend making their work auditable by humans to establish trust.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest limitation is our ability to give them context and verify their work. As agents can do longer and longer tasks, you don’t necessarily want to sit there watching every step. But you also need to know that they understood what you wanted and that the result is actually right.

Coding is a good example. An agent can produce a lot of code, but if a human has to review every line, you’ve moved the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing code. Tests help, but they don’t fully answer whether you built the right thing.

So I think a lot of the challenge is figuring out how to delegate: how to specify the goal, give the agent a way to check its own work, and have it come back to you when it needs a decision. The model getting smarter helps, but the way we work with it has to change too.

r001.rationale: The response names verifying agents’ work and knowing that the result is right as the biggest limitation, which conveys the trust concern.

r002.rationale: It says people need to know the result is right, but does not argue that agent work has little or no value when it cannot be trusted.

r003.rationale: It discusses human review as a bottleneck and agent self-checks, but does not recommend making work auditable by humans to establish trust.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest limitation is our ability to tell whether they’ve done the work correctly. If an agent can do an hour of work in a minute, but you still need an hour to review it, you haven’t gained very much.

So the question becomes: how do you make the result easy to verify? In coding, you can run tests, inspect the diff, and get fairly concrete feedback. For more open-ended tasks, it’s much harder to know whether the agent actually accomplished what you intended.

As agents do more, I think the bottleneck shifts from producing work to specifying what you want and checking the outcome. You need ways to give them feedback without having to watch every step.

r001.rationale: It identifies the biggest limitation as being able to tell whether an agent did the work correctly, which is a clear equivalent to trusting its outputs.

r002.rationale: It says lengthy review can erase much of the productivity gain, but does not argue that work has little or no value when a person cannot trust it.

r003.rationale: It recommends making results easy to verify and gives examples such as tests and diff inspection, but does not connect human auditing to establishing trust in the output.
